summary:
Roots for Tomorrow is a crop-rotation decision-support concept that combines NASA environmental data with local soil information, crop history, and farmer priorities. We developed a reproducible NASA POWER data analysis, a proposed comparison method, and an interface concept to help farmers explore their current cropping strategy alongside two alternatives.
Using ten years of NASA POWER data for a reference point in Uberaba, Brazil, we found that approximately 87% of average annual rainfall occurs between October and March. This regional historical pattern illustrates why rotation planning must consider seasonal water availability.
Our proposed tool compares strategies through water needs, soil cover, costs, and practical constraints, explaining the evidence, trade-offs, and missing information behind each option. Recommendations would require review by farmers and agronomists.
The project addresses the challenge by translating NASA data into understandable, locally grounded choices. It aims to support healthier soils and more resilient farms while making uncertainty visible. The next step is to implement and validate the comparison tool with farmers and agricultural experts.
details: Roots for Tomorrow helps farmers explore crop rotations that respond to seasonal water availability while considering soil protection, costs, and local farming conditions. We developed a reproducible NASA POWER data analysis and a visual interface concept. The comparison application is the next stage of development. How it works The proposed tool combines a farm’s location, crop history, soil test results, growing calendar, available equipment, budget, and farmer priorities with NASA environmental data. It compares the existing cropping strategy with two alternatives, explaining potential benefits, trade-offs, supporting evidence, and information gaps. Our initial analysis used 3,653 days of NASA POWER rainfall and maximum-temperature data from 2015–2024 for a reference point in Uberaba, Brazil. Approximately 87% of average annual rainfall in this sample occurred between October and March, illustrating the importance of aligning crop calendars with seasonal water availability. These data represent regional historical conditions, not field measurements or forecasts. Future integrations could add regional soil-moisture information from SMAP and vegetation-cover observations from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS). These integrations have not yet been implemented. Benefits and intended impact The project aims to make environmental information easier to use in agricultural planning. Farmers could explore diversification and cover-crop options while understanding their costs, water requirements, and management implications. Our intended impact is better-informed decisions that support soil protection and farm resilience. Water savings, income gains, and improvements in soil health remain hypotheses requiring field validation. The tool would support—not replace—farmer experience and agronomic expertise. Tools and development We used Python to process NASA POWER API responses, validate missing values, and calculate rainfall summaries. Matplotlib produced the rainfall visualization, and ReportLab generated the presentation PDFs. Pillow and FFmpeg supported the animated demonstration. AI tools assisted with research, coding, writing, conceptual imagery, and synthetic narration; the numerical rainfall evidence came from NASA POWER. The proposed application would use Python and Streamlit, locally cached data, documented comparison rules, and PDF summaries. No specialized hardware was required for the current deliverables. Creative approach and design considerations Our creative contribution is to connect environmental evidence with a farmer’s actual choices: compare three strategies, adjust priorities, and understand why an option may be suitable—or why there is insufficient information to assess it. We considered seasonal rainfall, differences in dataset resolution, soil conditions, crop calendars, market access, equipment, costs, and uncertainty. We also recognized that cover crops consume water and require careful management. A proposed pilot with farmers, agronomists, and a cooperative would evaluate usability and comparison quality before assessing longer-term field outcomes.
